Also note: this Prometheus plugin is only declared in the **Phase 1** KIC config (`kong-plugins.yaml`) — the Phase 2 docker-compose `kong.tmpl.yml` used locally for `triage`/`claims`/`fhir` has no Prometheus (or any metrics) plugin configured at all. `docs/phase2/requirements.md` R15 separately commits to "Metrics via Micrometer/Prometheus (Java) and Prometheus (Python) → Google Managed Prometheus (already declared in `kong-values.yaml`)" — i.e., the Phase 2 plan text references the Phase 1 Kong Prometheus declaration as the shared observability backend, but I found no Phase-2-service-level (triage/claims/fhir app-level, non-Kong) Prometheus exporter code in this pass — worth double-checking against another agent's findings if one specifically searched app-level `/metrics` endpoints in `triage-service`/`claims-service`. ## 5. fhir-service / claims-service error-shape conventions The commit log confirms the "three quirks" reference: `ceffc27 feat(phase4 M4): the three quirks -- pagination, required params, error shape` (in `epic-emulator`, not fhir-service/claims-service directly) — quirk **C** is "Error shape," implemented by `EpicOperationOutcome` (`epic-emulator/README.md:113-116`): > "**C — Error shape.** `EpicOperationOutcome` builds the `OperationOutcome` body used by quirk B's rejection and by the auth gate's `401` (upgraded from M2's plain JSON). Deliberately **not** applied to `TokenController`'s own OAuth2 token-endpoint errors — different protocol layer, different standard shape (decision E14)." **Across the repo there are actually three different, unreconciled error-shape conventions**, not one unified pattern: 1. **FHIR `OperationOutcome`** (HL7 standard shape: `issue[].severity` / `issue[].code` / `issue[].diagnostics`, `application/fhir+json`) — used by `claims-service`'s `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` for malformed-claim rejection (400) and by `epic-emulator`'s `EpicOperationOutcome` for its quirks. `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` docstring: distinguishes a **denial** (a decision about a valid claim, belongs in the audit trail) from a **malformed request** (not a claim at all, "must leave no trace") — deliberately not persisted/audited the same way. Field-level violations are explicitly sorted `(field, message)` for determinism, echoed as `OperationOutcome.issue[].diagnostics`; unparseable bodies get a generic message with no payload echo, "since claims are treated as PHI (R14)." `fhir-service` (HAPI FHIR JPA server) also returns `OperationOutcome` by default for its own errors (standard HAPI behavior). 2. **FastAPI default `{"detail": "..."}`** — `triage-service/src/triage/main.py` uses plain `HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...)` (404 patient/medication not found, 502 FHIR error) with no structured error-type field. 3. **A custom structured JSON shape** — `provider-registry-service/src/provider_registry/errors.py`: `{"error_type": ..., "message": ...}` (optionally `field`), with dedicated FastAPI exception handlers per error class (`not_found` → 404, `upstream_unavailable` → 503, plus a validation handler and a DB-operational handler) — this is the repo's "three error-taxonomy classes" referenced in `docs/testing-guide.md:141`. **Implication for the agent tier:** there is no single existing error-shape standard to mirror. FHIR-surface-facing services (claims-service, epic-emulator, fhir-service) converge on `OperationOutcome`; the two internal Python microservices diverge from each other (plain `detail` string vs. structured `error_type`/`message`). A fail-closed agent-tier REVIEW outcome should pick deliberately — e.g., mirror `OperationOutcome` if it's meant to be FHIR-audit-storable (like triage's own `RiskAssessment` response), or mirror `provider-registry-service`'s `{error_type, message}` taxonomy if it's an internal-API-only concern — and should document that choice, since the repo itself doesn't have one converged convention to inherit implicitly. ## 6. Queue / deadline / timeout / circuit-breaker patterns No circuit breaker is implemented anywhere in the deterministic tier — it is explicitly deferred. `HttpTriageClient.java:24`: **"Adding a circuit breaker here is follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy."** (I.e., the fail-closed *policy* — UNKNOWN on any failure — already covers correctness; a circuit breaker would only be a latency/throughput optimization on top of it.) Timeout conventions found (`grep -rnE "deadline|timeout|asyncio\.wait_for|circuit.?breaker|Queue\(" triage-service claims-service fhir-service gateway`): - **`claims-service` → `triage-service` HTTP call** (`HttpTriageClient.java:32-34,50-51`): `connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` at the `HttpClient` level, plus a per-request `timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(20))`. Both a connect-phase and an overall-request deadline are set explicitly, and — critically — a timeout is caught by the same `catch (Exception e)` block that maps to `RiskLevel.UNKNOWN` (line 76-79), so a timeout is treated identically to any other transport failure under the fail-closed policy, not as a special "assume safe" case. - **`claims-service` → `fhir-service`** (`HapiFhirClient.java:25`): `ctx.getRestfulClientFactory().setSocketTimeout(20_000)` — same 20s order of magnitude. - **`fhir-service` (HAPI/Spring config)**: `application.yaml:227-228` / `application-cds.yaml:207-208`: `timeoutSeconds: 30`, `socketTimeout: 60` (for outbound calls HAPI itself makes, e.g. CDS Hooks/terminology); `application-neon.yaml:66-67`: DB pool `connection-timeout: 30000`, `idle-timeout: 600000`. - **Kong**: no explicit request-level timeout override found in the DB-less `kong.tmpl.yml`/`kong-plugins.yaml`/`kong-ingress.yaml` beyond Kong's own defaults; `kong-ingress.yaml:55-56` notes the old `proxy` (timeouts) field is deprecated in KIC v3+ and timeouts are now expected to live in the k8s Service annotations on `fhir-service/k8s/service.yaml` instead. - No `Queue`, `asyncio.wait_for`, or any queuing/backpressure primitive appears anywhere in `triage-service`, `claims-service`, or `fhir-service` — the Python `triage-service` is fully synchronous FastAPI with no explicit per-request timeout of its own (it relies on the *caller's* client-side timeout, i.e., `claims-service`'s 20s, to bound the interaction — there's no server-side deadline enforcement in `triage-service` itself). **Convention for the agent tier to match:** every existing cross-service call sets an explicit connect timeout distinct from an explicit overall-request timeout (5s/20s pattern), and treats a timeout as a first-class member of the *same* failure-handling branch as any other unrecoverable error (mapping straight to the fail-closed `UNKNOWN`/PEND outcome) — it is not a special "maybe retry, maybe assume okay" path. A circuit breaker is explicitly out of scope by design precedent ("follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy") — so if the Phase 5 plan wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, it should note this diverges from the stated repo precedent (timeouts + fail-closed mapping, no breaker) rather than presenting a breaker as consistent with existing practice.

Gateway (Kong) rate limiting There are **two separate Kong deployments** in this repo (per `gateway/README.md` and `docs/gateway-runbook.md`), and their rate-limiting posture differs: **Phase 1 (Kubernetes/Helm KIC, deployed today, fronts only `fhir-service`)** — `gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml`, `fhir-rate-limit` KongPlugin: ```yaml plugin: rate-limiting config: second: 10 # max 10 requests/sec (DoS/burst protection) day: 1000 # max 1000 requests/day (usage quota) policy: cluster # counters written to Neon (kongdb) on every request hide_client_headers: false error_code: 429 error_message: "API rate limit exceeded. Retry after the indicated period." ``` Attached via annotation on `kong-ingress.yaml:34`: `konghq.com/plugins: "fhir-key-auth,fhir-rate-limit"`, with the comment "Order matters: key-auth runs first (reject unauthenticated requests before rate-limiting counts them)." This is **fail-closed / block-over-limit**: exceeding either window returns HTTP `429` with `Retry-After`/`X-RateLimit-*` headers — no degrade mode, no silent shedding. **Phase 2 (DB-less docker-compose Kong, the "canonical Phase 2 gateway," fronts `/claims`, `/fhir`, `/triage`)** — `gateway/kong/kong.tmpl.yml`: only a `key-auth` plugin is configured. **No rate-limiting plugin exists on the Phase 2 gateway at all** — this is the gateway that fronts `triage-service` and `claims-service` locally/in the docker-compose topology. So today, rate limiting is scoped only to `fhir-service` via the older Phase 1 KIC deployment; `triage-service` and `claims-service` have no gateway-level rate limit. Consumer provisioning already anticipates an agent consumer: `gateway/README.md:405-411` lists suggested consumers including `mcp-agent` — "LLM orchestration layer" — but no rate-limit plugin is attached to it specifically anywhere in the repo. **A second, independent, in-process rate-limiting precedent exists** (not gateway-based) — `provider-registry-service/src/provider_registry/ratelimit.py`, `RateLimitMiddleware`: a sliding-window (deque-based, not token-bucket) per-caller-IP limiter, explicitly "defense-in-depth against a compromised/buggy internal caller," in-memory (resets per instance, doesn't coordinate across replicas — an accepted limitation). It is also fail-closed/block-over-limit: ```python if len(hits) >= self._max_requests: return JSONResponse(status_code=429, content={"error_type": "rate_limited", "message": "too many requests"}) ``` This is the closest existing analog to the plan's proposed client-side token-bucket: an application-level (not gateway) rate limiter that hard-rejects (429) rather than degrading — but note it's a sliding-window counter, not a token bucket, and every existing rate limiter in this repo (gateway and in-process) **blocks/rejects over limit**; none of them "alert but don't shed." The plan's "alert not auto-shed" design for the LLM-call limiter would be a **new** pattern relative to every rate-limiting precedent in the repo, worth flagging explicitly as a deliberate departure, not an extension of existing convention — especially in tension with the "never silently drop a care request" framing, since "alert only" on a paid, clinical-tier API means requests still go through uncapped in practice. ## 4. Kong / infra observability — Prometheus Yes, Prometheus is already wired into the **Phase 1** Kong config. `gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml:99-126`, `fhir-prometheus` (`KongClusterPlugin`, global scope): ```yaml plugin: prometheus config: status_code_metrics: true latency_metrics: true bandwidth_metrics: true upstream_health_metrics: true ``` `gateway/README.md:367-386` documents the endpoint (`kong-kong-metrics:8100/metrics`) and states scraping depends on enabling GKE Managed Prometheus — the "Known Limitations" section is explicit: **"Prometheus metrics are declared but not scraped until Google Cloud Managed Prometheus is enabled in GKE. The `/metrics` endpoint works immediately for manual inspection."** So Prometheus export exists and is documented but is not confirmed as actively scraped in the deployed environment. Also note: this Prometheus plugin is only declared in the **Phase 1** KIC config (`kong-plugins.yaml`) — the Phase 2 docker-compose `kong.tmpl.yml` used locally for `triage`/`claims`/`fhir` has no Prometheus (or any metrics) plugin configured at all. `docs/phase2/requirements.md` R15 separately commits to "Metrics via Micrometer/Prometheus (Java) and Prometheus (Python) → Google Managed Prometheus (already declared in `kong-values.yaml`)" — i.e., the Phase 2 plan text references the Phase 1 Kong Prometheus declaration as the shared observability backend, but I found no Phase-2-service-level (triage/claims/fhir app-level, non-Kong) Prometheus exporter code in this pass — worth double-checking against another agent's findings if one specifically searched app-level `/metrics` endpoints in `triage-service`/`claims-service`. ## 5. fhir-service / claims-service error-shape conventions The commit log confirms the "three quirks" reference: `ceffc27 feat(phase4 M4): the three quirks -- pagination, required params, error shape` (in `epic-emulator`, not fhir-service/claims-service directly) — quirk **C** is "Error shape," implemented by `EpicOperationOutcome` (`epic-emulator/README.md:113-116`): > "**C — Error shape.** `EpicOperationOutcome` builds the `OperationOutcome` body used by quirk B's rejection and by the auth gate's `401` (upgraded from M2's plain JSON). Deliberately **not** applied to `TokenController`'s own OAuth2 token-endpoint errors — different protocol layer, different standard shape (decision E14)." **Across the repo there are actually three different, unreconciled error-shape conventions**, not one unified pattern: 1. **FHIR `OperationOutcome`** (HL7 standard shape: `issue[].severity` / `issue[].code` / `issue[].diagnostics`, `application/fhir+json`) — used by `claims-service`'s `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` for malformed-claim rejection (400) and by `epic-emulator`'s `EpicOperationOutcome` for its quirks. `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` docstring: distinguishes a **denial** (a decision about a valid claim, belongs in the audit trail) from a **malformed request** (not a claim at all, "must leave no trace") — deliberately not persisted/audited the same way. Field-level violations are explicitly sorted `(field, message)` for determinism, echoed as `OperationOutcome.issue[].diagnostics`; unparseable bodies get a generic message with no payload echo, "since claims are treated as PHI (R14)." `fhir-service` (HAPI FHIR JPA server) also returns `OperationOutcome` by default for its own errors (standard HAPI behavior). 2. **FastAPI default `{"detail": "..."}`** — `triage-service/src/triage/main.py` uses plain `HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...)` (404 patient/medication not found, 502 FHIR error) with no structured error-type field. 3. **A custom structured JSON shape** — `provider-registry-service/src/provider_registry/errors.py`: `{"error_type": ..., "message": ...}` (optionally `field`), with dedicated FastAPI exception handlers per error class (`not_found` → 404, `upstream_unavailable` → 503, plus a validation handler and a DB-operational handler) — this is the repo's "three error-taxonomy classes" referenced in `docs/testing-guide.md:141`. **Implication for the agent tier:** there is no single existing error-shape standard to mirror. FHIR-surface-facing services (claims-service, epic-emulator, fhir-service) converge on `OperationOutcome`; the two internal Python microservices diverge from each other (plain `detail` string vs. structured `error_type`/`message`). A fail-closed agent-tier REVIEW outcome should pick deliberately — e.g., mirror `OperationOutcome` if it's meant to be FHIR-audit-storable (like triage's own `RiskAssessment` response), or mirror `provider-registry-service`'s `{error_type, message}` taxonomy if it's an internal-API-only concern — and should document that choice, since the repo itself doesn't have one converged convention to inherit implicitly. ## 6. Queue / deadline / timeout / circuit-breaker patterns No circuit breaker is implemented anywhere in the deterministic tier — it is explicitly deferred. `HttpTriageClient.java:24`: **"Adding a circuit breaker here is follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy."** (I.e., the fail-closed *policy* — UNKNOWN on any failure — already covers correctness; a circuit breaker would only be a latency/throughput optimization on top of it.) Timeout conventions found (`grep -rnE "deadline|timeout|asyncio\.wait_for|circuit.?breaker|Queue\(" triage-service claims-service fhir-service gateway`): - **`claims-service` → `triage-service` HTTP call** (`HttpTriageClient.java:32-34,50-51`): `connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` at the `HttpClient` level, plus a per-request `timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(20))`. Both a connect-phase and an overall-request deadline are set explicitly, and — critically — a timeout is caught by the same `catch (Exception e)` block that maps to `RiskLevel.UNKNOWN` (line 76-79), so a timeout is treated identically to any other transport failure under the fail-closed policy, not as a special "assume safe" case. - **`claims-service` → `fhir-service`** (`HapiFhirClient.java:25`): `ctx.getRestfulClientFactory().setSocketTimeout(20_000)` — same 20s order of magnitude. - **`fhir-service` (HAPI/Spring config)**: `application.yaml:227-228` / `application-cds.yaml:207-208`: `timeoutSeconds: 30`, `socketTimeout: 60` (for outbound calls HAPI itself makes, e.g. CDS Hooks/terminology); `application-neon.yaml:66-67`: DB pool `connection-timeout: 30000`, `idle-timeout: 600000`. - **Kong**: no explicit request-level timeout override found in the DB-less `kong.tmpl.yml`/`kong-plugins.yaml`/`kong-ingress.yaml` beyond Kong's own defaults; `kong-ingress.yaml:55-56` notes the old `proxy` (timeouts) field is deprecated in KIC v3+ and timeouts are now expected to live in the k8s Service annotations on `fhir-service/k8s/service.yaml` instead. - No `Queue`, `asyncio.wait_for`, or any queuing/backpressure primitive appears anywhere in `triage-service`, `claims-service`, or `fhir-service` — the Python `triage-service` is fully synchronous FastAPI with no explicit per-request timeout of its own (it relies on the *caller's* client-side timeout, i.e., `claims-service`'s 20s, to bound the interaction — there's no server-side deadline enforcement in `triage-service` itself). **Convention for the agent tier to match:** every existing cross-service call sets an explicit connect timeout distinct from an explicit overall-request timeout (5s/20s pattern), and treats a timeout as a first-class member of the *same* failure-handling branch as any other unrecoverable error (mapping straight to the fail-closed `UNKNOWN`/PEND outcome) — it is not a special "maybe retry, maybe assume okay" path. A circuit breaker is explicitly out of scope by design precedent ("follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy") — so if the Phase 5 plan wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, it should note this diverges from the stated repo precedent (timeouts + fail-closed mapping, no breaker) rather than presenting a breaker as consistent with existing practice.

# Phase 5 Critique — findings from the actual codebase and docs

Four parallel audits (mcp-agent code, claims-agent/Phase 2, Phase 4/Phase 5 docs + observability infra, deterministic-tier conventions). No planning below — just what's confirmed, what's wrong, and what needs a decision from you before any milestone doc gets written.

## What's clear and holds up

**The handoff doc's code claims about mcp-agent are all accurate.** `agent.py`'s hardcoded Anthropic client/model/token cap, `SYSTEM_PROMPT`, `run_query(messages)→messages` mechanics, REPL persistence vs. `--query` non-persistence, `tools.py`'s two tools — all verified line-for-line. Good foundation to build the report on later.

**The cloud-delivery-gap claim is accurate and well-documented**, quotable directly from `docs/phase2/plan.md`'s "⚠️ Cloud-delivery gap" callout and `decisions.md` D8: no root Terraform module, no `deploy-phase2.sh`, only per-service Cloud Run stubs. The "Phase 2 isn't more cloud-ready" reasoning is sound.

**The status-truthfulness incident is real**, commit `0fcc196` ("status truth, safety semantics, gateway runbook, ADR index") — a reviewer did catch Phase 2 asserting things the repo didn't support. That precedent is legitimate grounds for not casually reopening Phase 2.

**A fail-closed convention already exists and is load-bearing** in `claims-service`: `Severity{DENY,PEND,REVIEW,INFO}` / `Outcome{APPROVED,DENIED,PENDED,ROUTED_FOR_REVIEW}`, plus the documented "unknown ≠ safe" lesson (`docs/testing-guide.md`: *"Make 'I don't know' a distinct value"*). `REVIEW` is already a specific, defined status in this codebase, not a blank slate — the plan's "fail-closed to REVIEW" choice happens to align with it.

## Corrections needed

- **Phase 2 was never "tagged."** Only `phase1-v1` exists as a git tag. Phase 2's "done" status lives in prose (`docs/phase2/README.md`'s canonical statement), not a tag. If this word carries into a milestone doc, it repeats an error.
- **`HttpTriageClientTest`'s stub-server pattern lives in `claims-service` (Java), not `triage-service`.** Triage-service has no HTTP-client tests of its own (it's the server, not a client). Reusing that pattern for mcp-agent means porting a Java/JUnit idiom to Python — nothing equivalent exists in Python yet, and no stub-server library (`respx`, etc.) is a dependency anywhere.
- **The R15 ("OTel tracing wired") claim in Phase 2's own milestone table is itself inflated.** No `opentelemetry` or `micrometer` dependency exists in `claims-service`/`rxclaim-emulator`, no `traceId`/correlation-ID code anywhere. This is a second, uncaught instance of the same documentation-vs-code gap the reviewer flagged once already — worth deciding whether to fix in Phase 2's docs opportunistically or just note it and move on.

## The collision that needs your call first

**`docs/phase5/` already has content, and it isn't this.** The only file there — `phase4-testing-and-analysis.md`, on this exact branch — is explicitly labeled *"DRAFT... not a Phase 5 PRD itself,"* and its entire content is a post-merge Phase 4 safety review, headlined by a **live, unfixed clinical-safety bug**: `epic-emulator`'s 20-record pagination cap silently drops allergy records, flipping a HIGH-risk (do-not-dispense) conflict to LOW-risk (safe to dispense) when a patient has >20 allergies. The doc says this should be fixed "**before Phase 5 starts**," and separately proposes Phase 5 scope around decomposing `epic-emulator`, not agent hardening.

`docs/phase4/README.md` and `docs/README.md` both currently reserve "Phase 5" for that epic-emulator decomposition work — "no timeline set," but the slot isn't empty. Nothing in the roadmap reserves "Phase 6" either. So: is agent-platform-hardening now Phase 5 (superseding/absorbing the epic-emulator content) or a different phase number, and — separately from naming — does the open pagination bug need to be dealt with before or alongside this work, given it's a live false-negative on the exact drug-allergy-conflict check `mcp-agent` calls?

## Things the plan should align to rather than invent

- **The triage rule engine (`rules.py`) is not fail-closed** — an unrecognized drug silently falls through to the `LOW`/"safe to dispense" default. Fail-closed only exists one layer up, in `HttpTriageClient.java`'s wrapper (`UNKNOWN` never `LOW` on any failure/timeout/unrecognized response). **mcp-agent talks to triage-service directly, bypassing that Java wrapper entirely** — so today there is no fail-closed protection on that path at all; `tools.py` defaults to the string `"UNKNOWN"` only on parse failure, and nothing stops the LLM from recommending dispense anyway. This is a more concrete version of the "output safety" gap than the handoff doc's framing — worth having in view for M1.
- **PHI redaction has a real precedent to copy**: `provider-registry-service`'s `sanitize_location()` + structural (not scrub-after-the-fact) logging middleware. There's also a documented near-miss (`docs/developer-guide.md`): a design doc claimed a PHI-safety mechanism existed for five milestones before anyone checked — it didn't. Direct caution against writing "PHI-redact span attributes" in a plan without verifying it's wired.
- **A live, currently-open PHI exposure already exists**: Kong's `file-log` plugin logs raw request URIs (containing patient/member IDs) to stdout today, per `docs/gateway-runbook.md`'s own acknowledgment. Worth deciding whether Phase 5's observability/redaction work touches this opportunistically.
- **Timeout convention across the deterministic tier is consistent**: explicit connect-timeout + overall-timeout pairs (5s/20s), and a timeout is folded into the *same* fail-closed branch as any other failure — never a special "assume okay" path. `HttpTriageClient.java` explicitly defers circuit breakers as future work ("changes latency, not policy"). mcp-agent today has one flat 30s timeout, no distinct connect timeout, no retry. If M4 wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, that's a new pattern relative to repo precedent, not an extension of one.
- **Every existing rate limiter in the repo (Kong's `fhir-rate-limit`, provider-registry-service's in-process limiter) is fail-closed/block-over-limit (429).** None "alert without shedding." The plan's M4 proposal to alert-not-shed on the LLM call is a genuine departure from every precedent here — and arguably in tension with its own "never silently drop a care request" framing, since alert-only means the request still goes through uncapped. That needs an explicit rationale, not an implicit one.
- **No single error-shape convention exists to inherit** — FHIR `OperationOutcome` (claims-service, epic-emulator, fhir-service) vs. plain FastAPI `{"detail": ...}` (triage-service) vs. structured `{error_type, message}` (provider-registry-service) are three unreconciled shapes. M1's output contract needs to pick one deliberately and say why, not assume there's a repo standard.

## Other facts worth having before any milestone doc

- **claims-agent already has a `--no-llm` deterministic mode** (template-rendered explanation, no API key needed) that mcp-agent lacks — a real existing fallback pattern, potentially relevant to M1/M6's fail-closed design, that the handoff doc didn't mention.
- **Neither agent has any provider abstraction, memory persistence, or observability today** — both are equivalently minimal Anthropic-only scripts. The "carry to Phase 2's claims stack" premise is architecturally sound (nearly identical skeletons), but there's no existing asymmetry to exploit — it's a clean build for both.
- **Gateway-level observability is not a clean slate**: Kong's Prometheus plugin and a GKE-Managed-Prometheus `ServiceMonitor` are already declared (though not confirmed scraped) — but only on the Phase 1 KIC deployment, not the Phase 2 docker-compose Kong that fronts triage/claims locally, and not at the application/LLM level anywhere. M2 should probably feed that existing pipeline rather than stand up a parallel one.
- **The `oneOf`-schema-fragility memory concern doesn't apply to any tool schema that exists today** — both current tools (`get_patient_summary`, `assess_refill_risk`) are flat single/dual-string-param schemas with zero nesting. It's a forward-looking concern for whatever M1's enum-output tool or M5's cross-provider schemas end up shaped like, not a current bug to fix.

## What needs to be discussed (merging the handoff's §8 with what the audit surfaced)

1. **Phase numbering and the epic-emulator collision** (new, and probably the highest-priority one — it affects the branch/doc structure of everything else).
2. Relationship to the open pagination safety bug — block Phase 5 on it, run in parallel, or explicitly out of scope with a stated reason.
3. Enum set for the pilot surface + REVIEW semantics — now informed by `claims-service`'s existing `Severity`/`Outcome` vocabulary; decide whether to reuse it or diverge deliberately.
4. Whether the "alert not auto-shed" rate/cost control is intentional given it contradicts every existing rate-limiter's fail-closed posture.
5. Error-shape choice for the agent's fail-closed output (FHIR `OperationOutcome` vs. `{error_type, message}` vs. something new).
6. Whether M2 observability plugs into the existing (declared-but-unconfirmed) Kong/Managed-Prometheus pipeline or stands alone.
7. Whether to touch the live Kong PHI-in-logs exposure while doing PHI-redaction work, or leave it out of scope.
8. The rest of the original §8 list (session-store tech, "important" response definition, transport, RAG corpus, memory token-budget numbers) — unchanged, still open.

Doing it now is cheap (docs-only PR) and closes the loop honestly. Risk is low, but it does mean re-touching a "closed" phase's docs — which is exactly the thing you decided Phase 5 should *not* do for substantive work. I'd distinguish: **correcting a false status claim is not "reopening Phase 2's work"** — it's fixing a factual error, same class of edit as the original truthfulness commit. Worth stating that distinction explicitly in the PR description so it doesn't read as scope creep.

## 2. Resolve the Phase 5 naming collision

Then update `docs/README.md`'s roadmap table and `docs/phase4/README.md`'s "a future Phase 5 would decompose along whatever the coupling note shows" line to match.

My read: the epic-emulator-decomposition content is thin (one draft doc, no timeline, explicitly not a PRD) versus agent-hardening being a fully-scoped multi-milestone effort — so renumbering epic-emulator work to Phase 6 (or folding it into a Phase 4b/4c alongside the safety-bug fix) and giving agent-hardening the Phase 5 slot is probably the lower-friction path. ## 3. Relocate the existing `docs/phase5/phase4-testing-and-analysis.md`

Once step 2 is decided, move that file to live under `docs/phase4/` (it's substantively a Phase 4 follow-up analysis, not Phase 5 content) or renumber it to match wherever epic-emulator-decomposition work lands.

Also worth checking whether the current branch name (`docs/phase5-readiness-assessment`) itself should be renamed/reused or abandoned in favor of a fresh branch for the real Phase 5 kickoff docs — the branch name currently promises something that isn't what you're about to build there.

Right now the bug lives only in that one draft doc. Add it as a numbered entry in `docs/phase4/decisions.md` (or a new `docs/phase4/known-issues.md` if the repo doesn't already have a lighter-weight "open bug" doc type) and keep the warning banner already in `docs/phase4/README.md` pointing at it.

The repo already has a `decisions.md` convention (lettered/numbered entries like D8, E10) — reuse that shape rather than inventing a new doc type; that matches existing convention more cleanly than a new `known-issues.md`. Low risk, high value, should happen regardless of how step 2 resolves.

## 5. Document the mcp-agent fail-closed gap we found this session

The finding that mcp-agent calls `triage-service` directly, bypassing `HttpTriageClient`'s fail-closed wrapper, with nothing in code stopping the LLM from recommending dispense on an `UNKNOWN` risk code — currently exists only in this conversation. Write it up as a decision/known-gap entry, most naturally as an input to Phase 5 M1 rather than retroactively into Phase 1 docs (Phase 1 is tagged `phase1-v1` as "done" — same tension as step 1, but here the gap is genuinely new work, not a false status claim, so it belongs in the *next* phase's docs, not a correction to the last one).

**Critique:** I'd deliberately keep this out of Phase 1's docs even though the bug lives in Phase-1-owned code — editing a tagged "done" phase to add a newly-discovered gap is a different (and messier) thing than fixing a factual status error, and it's exactly the kind of scope-widening CLAUDE.md tells me to avoid without being asked. Better home: a "known gaps this milestone must address" section in whatever `docs/phase5/plan.md` M1 ends up being — it's real input, not phase-2-style status cleanup.

## 6. Git tagging

Convention observed: `phase1-v1` marks a snapshot taken *at a phase boundary*, not "phase complete" in the abstract. To match that pattern, `phase2-v1` and `phase3-v1` would need to be tagged retroactively at the actual merge commits where each phase's last milestone landed (found via `git log`, not just tagged at current HEAD) — before Phase 5 starts would be the natural boundary for a `phase4-v1`-or-whatever-it's-called tag, **except Phase 4 is explicitly not fully closed** (open safety bug), so tagging it as a clean boundary right now would recreate the exact status-truthfulness problem in a git tag instead of a doc.

**Critique:** This is the step I'd push back on hardest as "not yet." Retroactively tagging Phase 2/3 has real value (consistent, navigable history) but is pure completeness/hygiene, not blocking anything — I'd rank it lowest priority of the six. Tagging Phase 4 right now is actively inadvisable given the open bug; if you want a Phase-4 boundary tag at all, it should wait until step 4's bug is fixed (or the tag name should honestly encode "milestones merged, safety finding open," which is awkward enough that it argues for just waiting). Also note: tags that get pushed to `origin` are a shared-state action — per your own git rules I'd confirm before pushing any of them, even though creating a local tag alone is cheap/reversible.

## Sequencing summary

Steps 1 and 4 are independent and safe to do now. Step 2 is a decision that gates 3. Step 5 can happen alongside 2/3 since it doesn't depend on the naming outcome. Step 6 is optional hygiene, lowest priority, and should explicitly exclude Phase 4 until the bug's fixed.

# Decision Index (ADR-style)

Every architectural decision on this project, in one auditable list: what was decided, its
status, what superseded it, and where the full rationale lives.

**This page is an index, not a rewrite.** Each decision's reasoning already exists in a
normative document; duplicating it here would create two versions that drift. Follow the link
for the *why*. Read this page for *what was decided, and whether it still holds*.

Two families:

- **D1–D8 — Deviations from the source PRD.** Where what we agreed to build differs from the
  DRAFT PRD. Full table: [`requirements.md` → Deviations](./requirements.md#deviations-from-the-prd).
- **C1–C4 — Cloud, security & scalability decisions.** Made during design, before build. Full
  table: [`README.md`](./README.md).

Status values: **Accepted** (in force) · **Superseded** (replaced — successor named) ·
**Partially delivered** (accepted, but the repo does not yet match — the gap is named).

---

## D — Deviations from the PRD

|---|---|---|---|

**Status:** DRAFT — a testing/analysis exercise performed after Phase 4 (M1–M5) was complete and
merged, not a Phase 5 PRD itself. Everything below is either something actually run against live
services, or a review of actual merged code — nothing here is speculative.
**Method:** three passes over the same completed system, each asking a different question of it —

severity, not by which hat found them.

---

## 0. Headline finding — read this first

**`epic-emulator`'s pagination quirk (M4, quirk A) can cause a real, silent, false-negative

through `epic-emulator`, because `client/clinical`'s FHIR client (used by `triage-service`) never
follows FHIR's `Bundle.link[relation=next]` pagination link; it assumes one page is the whole
answer. If the clinically-relevant allergy (in this test: penicillin) happens to fall on page 2, it
is silently dropped **before triage-service's rule engine ever sees it**.

| | Direct to `fhir-service` | Via `epic-emulator` |
|---|---|---|

## 4. Recommendations for Phase 5 (and one thing before it)

### 4.0 Before Phase 5 starts: fix or mitigate §1.1

This is a live safety-relevant bug in merged code, not a Phase 5 backlog item. Two real fix
options, not mutually exclusive:

1. **The durable fix:** make `client/clinical`'s FHIR client follow `Bundle.link[relation=next]`
   when fetching medications/allergies. This is the correct behavior against *any* real FHIR
   server, not just `epic-emulator` — Phase 4 only surfaced a pre-existing latent gap in Phase 1
   code, it didn't create the underlying assumption. This does touch `triage-service`'s dependency
   (`client/clinical`), which is more invasive than anything Phase 4 itself touched.
2. **The fast mitigation:** raise `epic.quirks.pagination.max-count`'s default well above any
   realistic patient record count (or make quirk A's cap configurable per-deployment with a safe
   default), so the emulator's own demonstrability doesn't come at the cost of plausible patients
   silently losing data. This doesn't fix the underlying client gap (a real Epic server could still
   paginate at a value the client doesn't expect) but closes the immediate hole.

**This wasn't fixed as part of this analysis — it's flagged for an explicit decision** on priority
and approach before treating Phase 4 as fully closed.

### 4.1 Testing policy: add consequence-level tests, not just mechanism-level ones

For any quirk or backfill that changes response *shape or content*, require at least one test that
exercises it through the same client code path a real consumer uses (as `e2e/
test_epic_emulator_acceptance.py` already does for the happy path) with a realistic *volume* of
data, not just a realistic *shape* of data. §1.1 would have been caught by a 25-allergy fixture in
the existing e2e test.

### 4.2 Wire epic-emulator into CI

At minimum: a `phase4-java` job running `mvn -f epic-emulator/pom.xml test` on every PR (mirroring
`phase2-java`/`phase3` conventions already established), so this module's own test suite — once
§4.1 closes the coverage gap — actually runs automatically instead of depending on a developer
remembering to.

### 4.3 Decompose auth first, if/when Phase 5 decomposes at all

Per the coupling note: auth is evidence-backed as the cleanest split. Extension handling and
pagination should stay together unless a real pipeline contract is designed first. Error-shape
formatting needs an explicit home (shared library, or its own small service) rather than being
implicitly owned by "whichever area happened to build it first."

### 4.4 Resolve E10 if real Epic access ever becomes available

Every quirk/extension specific value in this module remains an unverified, structurally-plausible
placeholder (decision E10). If a future effort gets real Epic sandbox or documentation access, this
is the one item that would most change what's actually built here — including, possibly, the exact
pagination cap value that made §1.1 possible in the first place.

### 4.5 Update the demo guide, once §4.0 is resolved

Don't add Phase 4 to `docs/demo-guide.md` until §4.0 has a resolution — a demo built on the current
pagination behavior risks reproducing §2.3's exact scenario in front of a real audience.

39:| **E2** | `epic-emulator` is a **proxy in front of `fhir-service`**, not a standalone service with its own embedded FHIR store | ✅ Accepted | Chosen over the standalone alternative to keep `fhir-service`'s already-seeded data as the single source of truth — no duplicate fixture pipeline. Accepted tradeoff: both services must run together for any real test. Rationale: [`prd.md` §9](./prd.md#9-decisions-resolving-open-questions-using-best-judgement), [`design.md` §1](./design.md#1-target-architecture). |
40:| **E3** | New **top-level `epic-emulator/` directory**, own Maven build — not a submodule of `fhir-service` | ✅ Accepted | Matches this repo's existing per-service layout; follows the same shape as the same-repo `rxclaim-emulator` precedent (internal-only Spring Boot service emulating a real system's contract). Rationale: [`prd.md` §9](./prd.md#9-decisions-resolving-open-questions-using-best-judgement). |
41:| **E4** | Extension emulation is **closed to Medication and AllergyIntolerance only**, tied to the existing prescription-refill-risk-triage reference workflow — not "any Epic extension" | ✅ Accepted | Bounds the module's scope to a concrete, testable slice instead of an open-ended surface. Rationale: [`prd.md` §1/§3](./prd.md#1-problem-statement). |
42:| **E5** | Quirk emulation is **closed to exactly three named quirks** — pagination/`_count` behavior, a required search-parameter combination, and `OperationOutcome` error-shape deviations — no open "quirks" backlog | ✅ Accepted | The three were chosen to sample different layers of API interaction (getting results back / what you're allowed to ask for / how errors are reported), not three variations on one theme. This is the concrete mechanism keeping Phase 4 sized in days, not weeks. Rationale: [`prd.md` §1](./prd.md#1-problem-statement), [`design.md` §6](./design.md#6-quirks--concrete-pinned-choices-starting-design-pending-validation). |
43:| **E6** | `triage-service` and `claims-service` decision logic is **explicitly excluded** from `epic-emulator` — the acceptance case (FR9) *exercises* `triage-service` through the proxy, it does not absorb or duplicate either service's rules | ✅ Accepted | Rejects an earlier proposal to bundle both services' functionality into the same monolith as the three capability areas. Both are already independently built and validated (Phase 1/Phase 2); Epic emulation is a protocol/format concern, not a clinical or claims-decision concern, and duplicating that logic would create a second, driftable copy. Rationale: [`prd.md` §3/§9](./prd.md#3-non-goals-this-phase). |
44:| **E7** | Extensions round-trip via **read-time backfill only** — reads inject a default Epic extension when one isn't already present; writes pass through unchanged, since `fhir-service` already stores arbitrary extensions with no special handling needed | ✅ Accepted | Satisfies "no new fixture pipeline" (PRD G4) with the least new code. Rationale: [`design.md` §5/§14](./design.md#5-extension-handling--concrete-approach). |
45:| **E8** | Auth-client registration is **dev-simple** — a config-file/in-memory JWK registration, no approval workflow or real vendor procurement process | ✅ Accepted | Matches the PRD's instruction to assume easy developer access; mirrors the *shape* of Epic's real backend-services flow (a client presents a public key) without the real-world overhead. Rationale: [`design.md` §4/§14](./design.md#4-auth-flow--concrete-contract). |
46:| **E9** | **No separate `plan.md`** — the milestone plan lives inside `design.md` (§12) | ✅ Accepted | Follows Phase 3's consolidation (Phase 2 had kept `requirements.md`/`plan.md` separate; Phase 3 folded that split into `prd.md`/`design.md`). Rationale: [`design.md` §14](./design.md#14-decisions-resolving-open-questions-using-best-judgement). |
47:| **E10** | The specific Epic documentation version to target for conformance, and the exact real values behind each quirk/extension (§6's table), are **not yet pinned** | 🟡 Partially delivered | M2 made one real attempt: `fhir.epic.com/Documentation?docId=oauth2` is genuinely public (no login), dated "Last updated: October 31, 2025," with a menu entry for backend OAuth 2.0 — but the specific technical parameters (JWT claim details, scope format, rate limits) are rendered behind interactive navigation, not retrievable by a plain page fetch. No account registration was attempted (an inherently human step). M2's auth flow was instead built directly against the public, normative **SMART Backend Services** spec (HL7/SMART Health IT) — a legitimate independent source, not a stand-in. The gap: Epic's own specific parameter values, and `design.md` §6's quirk table, remain "structurally representative," not "confirmed against Epic's own docs." Rationale: [`design.md` §7](./design.md#7-authoritative-documentation--the-one-open-action-item). |
48:| **E11** | Client-assertion signing supports **RS384 only** — the spec's other allowed algorithm, ES384 (EC keys), is not implemented | ✅ Accepted | Found while building M2: supporting EC keys too would add a second key-handling path in `ClientAssertionValidator` for marginal value at this stage. Documented as a known simplification, not a silent gap — worth revisiting only if a real Epic sandbox test ever requires ES384. Rationale: [`design.md` §4/§14](./design.md#4-auth-flow--concrete-contract). |
49:| **E12** | Extension emulation concretely targets **`MedicationRequest`**, not the generic "Medication" the PRD names | ✅ Accepted | Found while building M3: checked what the reference workflow actually reads rather than assuming — `triage-service`/`client/clinical` query `GET /MedicationRequest?patient=...&status=active`, never the `Medication` catalog resource. The PRD's "Medication" stays as higher-level category language; `design.md` §5 now pins the concrete resource type, same pattern as §6 pinning concrete quirk specifics. Rationale: [`design.md` §5](./design.md#5-extension-handling--concrete-approach). |
50:| **E13** | Pagination continuation (quirk A) uses an **opaque, in-memory server-side token** (`Map<token, realUrl>`), not a self-describing one (e.g. base64 or signed) | ✅ Accepted | Simpler, and there was never a reason for the caller to be able to inspect or reconstruct the real URL — an opaque lookup is the more faithful emulation of "you must follow the link verbatim" anyway. Pagination cap default (20, `epic.quirks.pagination.max-count`) is a demonstrably-below-typical-defaults value, not derived from any real Epic-documented number — still unverified per E10. Rationale: [`design.md` §6/§14](./design.md#14-decisions-resolving-open-questions-using-best-judgement). |
51:| **E14** | Quirk C's `OperationOutcome` shape is applied only to rejections on the **FHIR API surface** (quirk B, the M2 auth gate) — deliberately **not** to `TokenController`'s own OAuth2 token-endpoint errors | ✅ Accepted | Wrapping an OAuth2 error in a FHIR resource would be a category mismatch; real Epic's token endpoint returns standard OAuth2 errors too, not FHIR resources. `TokenController`'s `error`/`error_description` shape is intentionally unchanged. Rationale: [`design.md` §6](./design.md#6-quirks--concrete-pinned-choices-built-in-m4-values-still-pending-validation), [`quirks/EpicOperationOutcome`](../../epic-emulator/src/main/java/com/healthcare/epic/quirks/EpicOperationOutcome.java). |
52:| **E15** | `BearerAuthFilter` accepts a valid token via an **`apikey` header**, as a fallback to `Authorization: Bearer` | ✅ Accepted | Found for real while building M5: `triage-service`'s FHIR client (`client/clinical`) can only ever send an `apikey` header — it has no extensibility point for an arbitrary `Authorization` header, and editing it would violate the "zero code changes to triage-service" non-goal. `apikey` is this repo's own pre-existing Kong-gateway convention (already read/forwarded by `triage-service`), not something invented for this — the token is still obtained through the real SMART Backend Services flow, only how it's carried differs. This is what made the M5 acceptance case achievable at all. Rationale: [`design.md` §8](./design.md#8-integration-with-the-existing-platform). |

# Decision Index (ADR-style)

Every architectural decision for Epic Emulator, in one auditable list: what was decided, its
status, and where the full rationale lives. Modeled directly on
[`docs/phase3/decisions.md`](../phase3/decisions.md) — same status vocabulary, same convention.

**This page is an index, not a rewrite.** Each decision's reasoning already exists in
[`prd.md`](./prd.md) or [`design.md`](./design.md); duplicating it here would create two versions
that drift. Follow the link for the *why*. Read this page for *what was decided, and whether it
still holds*.

Status values: **Accepted** (in force) · **Superseded** (replaced — successor named) ·
**Partially delivered** (accepted, but the repo does not yet match — the gap is named).

**Phase 4 is complete — M1 through M5 are all built** (see [`README.md`](./README.md)'s canonical
status). E1–E9 and E11–E15 are now verified against real, tested code, and E15 specifically
against a live, two-service, end-to-end run (`e2e/test_epic_emulator_acceptance.py`) — not just
unit-level Java tests. E9 is a documentation-format decision, not code. **E10 remains genuinely
partial** — M2 made one real, verifiable attempt (§7/design.md) and confirmed the Epic
documentation site is real and public at a shell level, but the Epic-specific technical parameters
were not retrievable that way; M2's auth flow, and M4's quirk specifics, were built against the
public base SMART Backend Services spec and structurally-representative placeholders instead,
which is legitimate but not the same as Epic-confirmed — **this is the one decision Phase 5 (or
whoever picks up real Epic sandbox access) should revisit first.** E11 records the RS384-only
scoping choice found while building M2; E12 records that M3's concrete resource-type scoping is
`MedicationRequest`, not the PRD's more generic "Medication"; E13/E14 record M4's pagination-token
and error-shape-scoping choices; E15 (new) records the `apikey`-header auth fallback found while
building M5's acceptance case — the one real, unforeseen gap between M2's auth gate and the PRD's
"zero code changes to triage-service" non-goal, resolved without touching triage-service. The
coupling note (PRD G6) is [`coupling-note.md`](./coupling-note.md), not restated here.
